Choosing Your Fence

Three ways to build it — plainly compared, so you can pick what fits your yard, your budget, and how long you want it to last.

Every fence we build is solid. The difference between our three options comes down to the wood, the posts, and how many years and seasons you want it to keep looking its best. Here's an honest look at each — the good and the trade-offs — so there are no surprises.

The Three Options

Good, better, and best — every one a real privacy fence.

Option 1 · Value

Pressure-Treated Pine

6' pine pickets & rails · pressure-treated pine 4×4 posts

What's good about it

  • Lowest upfront cost — the budget-friendly way to get a full privacy fence.
  • Pressure treatment is guaranteed by the mill against rot and insect damage, often for 20+ years.
  • Strong and readily available, so repairs and matching boards are easy down the road.
  • A smart pick for large runs, rentals, or when budget is the deciding factor.

The trade-offs

  • Pine moves. As it dries it tends to warp, cup, and check (surface cracks) more than cedar — sometimes within the first months.
  • The treatment stops rot, but it does not stop warping or shrinking — that's the nature of the wood.
  • Wood 4×4 posts are in the ground, where wood is most vulnerable over the long haul.
  • Wants staining sooner and a little more often to look its best and hold the line straight.
⚠️Warranty: None. Pine is our value build — a solid fence at the lowest price, offered without a workmanship guarantee.

A Fortress pressure-treated pine privacy fence — our value build.

Option 2 · Most Popular

Japanese Cedar

6' import cedar pickets w/ whitewood rails · 2-3/8" 16-gauge steel posts

What's good about it

  • A genuine step up from pine — more dimensionally stable, so it holds its shape and resists the warping and cupping pine is prone to.
  • Has natural resistance to rot and insects, and takes our oil stain beautifully for a clean, finished look.
  • Steel posts don't rot in the ground, so the part that usually fails first on a wood fence simply doesn't.
  • Fine, even grain with smaller, tighter knots than most softwoods.
  • The sweet spot: a real upgrade in looks and stability over pine, at a friendlier price than premium Western Red Cedar.

The trade-offs

  • Costs more than pine up front.
  • Here's the honest truth: "Japanese cedar" (sugi) isn't a true cedar — it's a related species. It has some natural decay resistance, but it's not as rot-resistant or as tough as Western Red Cedar, and quality can vary more board to board.
  • Keeping it stained matters more here than on Western Red — the stain is doing more of the protecting.
  • The whitewood rails aren't naturally rot-resistant — staining protects them.
✓Warranty: 3-year workmanship guarantee.

Japanese cedar pickets with whitewood rails on galvanized steel posts — our mid-grade build.

A finished Japanese cedar fence run.

Option 3 · Premium

Western Red Cedar

6' Western Red Cedar pickets & rails · 2-3/8" 13-gauge steel posts

What's good about it

  • The best-looking and longest-lasting wood we build with — the benchmark every other fence wood (including Japanese cedar) is measured against.
  • Its natural oils (plicatic acid) make it one of the most decay- and insect-resistant woods there is — genuinely more rot-resistant than Japanese cedar, all the way through both the pickets and the rails.
  • The most dimensionally stable wood here: it stays straight and resists warping, twisting, and cupping.
  • Heavy 13-gauge steel posts — nearly 50% thicker steel than standard — for maximum strength in wind and over time.
  • Rich, deep grain and color that holds stain beautifully; the strongest curb appeal and resale value.

The trade-offs

  • Highest upfront cost of the three.
  • Because it's a premium material, availability can occasionally affect lead time.
  • Want to trim the cost a little? We offer a save option that keeps the Western Red Cedar and steps the posts down to standard 16-gauge — still steel, still no rot, just a lighter wall.
  • Want to go the other way? We can step the posts up to Schedule 40 commercial-grade — the heaviest post we install — for maximum strength.
⭐Lifetime workmanship guarantee — when paired with a metal-framed gate. This is the only build we stand behind for life, and it's why: premium wood, the heaviest posts, and a gate that won't sag.

A Fortress Western Red Cedar privacy fence — our premium build.

Pickets compared

The real cost is per year, not up front

The cheapest fence isn't always the best value. A fence that costs a little more but lasts far longer is actually cheaper for every year you own it — and you only live through the mess and cost of replacing it once. Here's the honest way to think about it:

PineTypical lifespan ~15 yearsLowest price today
Shortest life
Japanese CedarTypical lifespan ~15–20 yearsMid price
Mid life
Western Red Cedar ⭐Typical lifespan 25–30+ years, backed by our lifetime workmanship guaranteeBest cost per year
Longest life, one install

Because Western Red Cedar can last roughly twice as long as pine, spreading its cost across all those extra years often makes it the lowest cost per year of the three — and it's the only one we guarantee for life. You buy it once, you stain it (no stripping, ever), and you're done. That's not us trying to sell up; it's just how the math works out over the life of a fence. Ask us to run the per-year numbers on your specific quote — we're happy to show you.

What untreated wood looks like over time

Left to weather, wood fades to gray and can warp or bow — you can see it here where a fresh board sits against the aged wood. Staining slows this on any fence, and the more durable the wood, the longer it holds. It's the clearest reason the longer-lasting builds are worth it: you replace them far less often.

A Word on Posts

The posts are the backbone. It's the part of a fence that most often fails first — so it's worth understanding.

Pressure-Treated Pine 4×4

Option 1

The budget choice. Treated to resist rot, but it's still wood in the ground — over many years, ground moisture is hard on any wood post, and it can shift or soften at the soil line.

2-3/8" 16-Gauge Steel

Standard on Option 2 · save option on Option 3

Galvanized steel that won't rot, period. Roughly a .065" wall — plenty strong for a standard residential privacy fence, and it eliminates the #1 long-term weak point of a wood fence.

2-3/8" 13-Gauge Steel

Premium · standard on Option 3

The heavy-duty post. At roughly a .095" wall it's nearly 50% thicker steel than 16-gauge — stiffer, more resistant to wind and impact, and a long-lasting support built to stand where thin posts eventually lean.

2-3/8" Schedule 40 — Commercial Grade

Heaviest option · commercial & high-wind

Our thickest post. Schedule 40 is true commercial/industrial pipe with a .154" wall — more than twice the steel of a 16-gauge post, and noticeably heavier than even 13-gauge. This is what goes in for tall fences, high-wind exposure, big drive gates, and commercial jobs where the fence has to take a beating and never move. If you want the strongest fence we can build, it starts here.

See the difference

A Word on Rails

The rails are the horizontal backbone the pickets nail to. They're hidden on the back of the fence — and they're where a lot of fences quietly fail.

SPF Rails

Builder-grade — what most new-construction fences use

SPF (spruce-pine-fir) is cheap framing lumber. Here's the catch: it is not naturally rot-resistant and it isn't really outdoor-grade. Untreated SPF is meant to be kept dry — out in the weather on a fence, the rails are the first thing to go soft and let the fence sag. It's the quiet weak point in a lot of builder-grade fences.

Pressure-Treated Pine Rails

A real step up

Pressure-treated pine is chemically treated to resist rot and insects, so it holds up outdoors far better than bare SPF. Treatment slows decay rather than stopping it entirely, but as a rail it's a genuine, dependable upgrade — and it's what we use on our pine build.

Western Red Cedar Rails

The best rail we build with

Cedar rails resist rot and insects naturally, through the wood's own oils — no treatment needed, and no weak link on the back of the fence. When the rails are as durable as the pickets, the whole fence lasts. This is why our premium build uses Western Red Cedar rails throughout.

💡Worth knowing: Most new-construction homes today go up with the affordable builder package — 16-gauge posts, SPF rails, and Japanese cedar pickets. It's a fine starter fence, but the SPF rails aren't outdoor-grade, so it doesn't tend to last. If you're replacing a builder fence that didn't hold up, the rails are usually why.

Rails compared

Sag-Proof Metal-Framed Gates

The upgrade that solves the #1 thing that goes wrong with fence gates.

Sag-Proof

Why most gates sag — and ours don't

A standard wood gate hangs on hinges that are lag-screwed into the wood. Over time those screws work against the wood grain: the fibers around them expand, loosen, and give — and the gate starts to sag, drag on the ground, and stop latching. It's the most common gate failure there is.

Our metal-framed gate is built on a welded steel frame and hinged directly to the steel posts with pipe hinges — no screws driven into wood to work loose. The whole gate hangs off steel, not off wood fibers. That's why we call it sag-proof: it swings true and latches right for the long haul.

It's also what unlocks our lifetime workmanship guarantee on the Western Red Cedar build — we can stand behind that fence for life because the gate, the usual weak point, is built not to fail.

About Our Stain

Staining isn't just for looks — it protects your investment and helps the wood last. But not all stain is the same, and it matters a great deal which kind goes on your fence.

We use only Wood Defender (by Standard Paints) or HueMiller — both 100% oil-based, penetrating stains. We don't use the water-based stains sold at the big-box stores, and here's why it matters to you:

Big-box stains tend to form a film on the surface of the wood. Films look fine at first, but over time they peel, crack, and flake — and once that starts, re-doing the fence means the messy, expensive job of stripping off the old coating first.

Our oil stains work differently. They soak into the wood instead of sitting on top, so there's no film to fail — they simply can't peel or crack. They protect the wood better from the inside, and they weather by slowly fading rather than flaking.

The payoff comes years down the road. When it's time to refresh the color, we don't strip anything. We just soft-clean the fence and apply a fresh coat right over the old one. No stripping, no scraping, no mess — and a far easier, cleaner job every time.

Wood DefenderBy Standard Paints — a Texas manufacturer since 1952. Oil-based, penetrating stain & sealer in one.
HueMiller100% oil-based penetrating stain. Same no-peel, no-strip, soak-in protection.

Cap & Trim: The Finished Look

The upgrade that turns a fence into a showpiece.

A standard privacy fence is just pickets and rails. Adding a cap and trim — a top cap board with a finish trim board beneath it — gives the fence a clean, framed, finished edge along the top. It hides the picket ends, adds strength, and gives the whole fence a custom, high-end look. Paired with a rich stain, it's the difference between a fence and a statement.

A stained board-on-board fence with cap and trim — built and finished by Fortress Fencing.

This one is board-on-board (pickets overlapped so there are no gaps, even as the wood moves) with our cap and trim and a full oil stain. Cap, trim, board-on-board, and stain are all available as upgrades on any of the three options — ask us what they'd look like on your build.

Common Questions

The things folks ask us most.

How long will my fence last?
It depends on the wood and the posts. A well-maintained pine fence commonly lasts around 15 years; cedar typically 20–30 years or more. Steel posts dramatically extend the life of any wood fence because the posts don't rot in the ground. Keeping up with stain makes a real difference on any of the three.
Do I really need to stain it?
Staining protects the wood and keeps the color — and with our penetrating oil stains it's an easy thing to keep up with. New pine especially benefits from staining sooner. Cedar has natural oils that buy you more time, but a good stain still extends its life and looks. Left unstained, any wood fence weathers to gray over time.
How often does it need re-staining?
Roughly every few years, depending on sun exposure and the look you want. Because our oil stain penetrates instead of forming a film, re-coating is simple: we soft-clean the fence and apply a fresh coat right over the last one — no stripping or scraping required.
Why steel posts instead of wood?
The posts are the part of a wood fence that most often fails first, because wood in the ground is exposed to constant moisture. Steel posts don't rot, so your fence stays straight and solid far longer. It's one of the biggest upgrades you can make to a fence's lifespan.
What's the difference between 16-gauge and 13-gauge posts?
Gauge is the thickness of the steel wall — and a lower number means thicker steel. 16-gauge (about .065") is a strong, dependable post for a standard residential fence. 13-gauge (about .095") is nearly 50% thicker, so it's stiffer and more resistant to wind, impact, and time. Both are galvanized and won't rot.
My builder just put up a fence — why would I need a new one?
Most new-construction homes go up with the affordable builder package: 16-gauge posts, SPF (spruce-pine-fir) rails, and Japanese cedar pickets. It looks fine on day one and it's a reasonable starter fence — but SPF rails aren't really outdoor-grade lumber, so those fences tend not to last. When a builder-grade fence starts sagging or failing, it's usually the rails giving out. Stepping up to pressure-treated or cedar rails and steel posts is what makes a fence go the distance.
Can I mix and match — like cedar with the cheaper posts?
Absolutely. These three options are a starting point, not a rulebook. A common example is our Western Red Cedar "save option," which keeps the premium cedar but uses standard 16-gauge posts to trim the cost. Tell us your priorities and we'll build the combination that fits.
What about gates, caps, and trim?
All of it is available on any of the three options — decorative post caps, a finished trim/cap board along the top, custom gates, and upgraded hardware. Ask about our sag-proof metal-framed gate, too — it's the gate that won't droop or drag over time. These are listed as optional upgrades on your estimate so you can add exactly what you want.
What warranty comes with my fence?
It depends on the build. Our pine option is offered without a workmanship warranty. Japanese cedar carries a 3-year workmanship guarantee. Western Red Cedar carries our lifetime workmanship guarantee when it's paired with a metal-framed gate. Wood-framed gates with standard hinges carry a 90-day warranty; the metal-framed gate is the sag-proof upgrade. We'll spell out exactly what applies to your build on your estimate.
How do I get an exact price?
Every yard is different — length, gates, terrain, and access all factor in — so we price each job for your specific property. This guide is about understanding the differences; your estimate has the numbers. Give us a call and we'll get you taken care of.
